pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press
18 East 48th Street
Newyork.                                Newyork, 29th Jan. 1941.

Dear Hanna, dear Manfred,
I hope you did not expect a cable after our
meeting with Eva, but Stefan thought I should wait until I had some-
thing definite to tell. This also can only be a preliminary report
as nothing is decided yet and I am now waiting for neutral reports
and references of the different places in question. I have been at
Croton on the Hudson - three quarters of an hour by train from Newyork -
and seen Mrs. Schaeffer, the wife of the German poet Albrecht Schaeffer
who came here also as refugees and who has a large house and in addition
to her many children (three in school age, two grown up and one appa-
rently ill and not with them) about twelve to fifteen children in all
different ages. There is none exactly in Eva's age, but two girls of
ten and a few boys of twelve and thirteen. I had an excellent impression
of Mrs. Schaeffer, the first women who in her way of thinking and
speaking reminded me a little of you and with whom I could discuss
things as we would have done it. The house is already a little small
for them and they are planning to build one or two more rooms in March.
It is a little ~~prx~~ packed, therefore, and very plain, but I don't
think this would matter. The house itself is situated in a large
garden, has vegetable garden, orchard and fowls, and the children are
supposed to help a little with all that. They also have to make their
own beds, clean their shoes and help serving at table. There are also
different hours where instead of English they are supposed to speak
French or German. Personally I liked all these arrangements, and Mrs.
Sch.'s husband, the poet, does not hinder in any way as he lives across
the road in a tiny little garden house and does some poetry so pure
that it goes above our heads. As to religion, they have some christian
and a few Jewish children. They themselves are Christians but besides
a general "christian spirit" there is no religious service or influence
in the house. I am hesitant, however, about the choice of schools
should I decide to put her there. There are two, one very modern and
"progressive" ( a term which I have not yet been able to analyse pro-
perly except that it has something to do with awakening the creative
in the child and group work), the other the Croton public school. I
am expecting reports about these two from an Educational Advisory
Committee where I have been today. The problem is that most of the
children at Mrs. Sch.'s - 13 out of 15 - go the progressive school,
and that, if we do not like the idea of that school, it seems a little
doubtful whether she/feel happy to go to the other. - This is the one
possibility which would we are still examining from all points of
view. The other one is a boarding school of about forty girls, also
near Newyork which has been recommended to me by friends of my sister-
in-laws. I have met the proprietress here in Newyork to-day, a little
the Galician Jewish type but quite civilized and clever. I shall go
and see the school on Sunday and cannot form a judgment before. I shall
also try to get information about it through that committee. That would
be again anxxx a completely American surrounding, and I would have to
find out what the teaching is worth. - Number three is that I have
written to Einstein's and am expecting their answer. - Number 4 is
an offer of an immigrated doctor whose wife has two nearly grown-up
children and would like to have a younger one again in the house.

2

I shall meet her to-morrow and if I do not get an excellent
impression leave this matter entirely. They are supposed to be very
cultured and nice people, and I shall be very careful this time if I
decide for a family. - - On account of all this looking around
and enquiring here and there I have not yet seen Eva these last days,
but will do so soon. In any case I can reassure you again, that she
is not at all unhappy at Salmon's and that there is no hurry for
taking her away. Only as we will probably leave Newyork xxxxxxxx
at the end of next week I want to settle her first. As to asking her-
self what the woud like and where she would like to go, we have decided
against it, she is still too small to know, and we know her sufficient-
ly to guess what she would like and what is the right thing for her.
I must finish for to-day, we are going out, and Stefan
has already written his part. - We are still a little tired, the
change of air and temperature seems not yet quite overcome by our
physical beings. Otherwise we feel quite alright here, only the
friends know that we have arrived and not yet the "old acquaintances".

Kindest regards, best love, follow
Stefan's wish that you go to Bath for a while,

Lotte

I have spoken to Mrs. Haas and she gave me the address of this
Advisory Committee where I have been. I hope to see the boys
before I leave. It is out of town and I must make the appointment
a few days before as Mrs. Haas seems very busy with some charity
affairs.
pages.notes: Typoskript, Unterschrift und handschriftlicher Zusatz von Lotte Zweig in violetter Tinte.
